Your statement lasted seven minutes. The TV broadcast cut away in the third minute. In the next day's papers, your final statement was down to one sentence, “I plead guilty here before the whole Party, the whole army and the people of the whole country.”

The court clerk took down all seven minutes. The transcript went into a kraft-paper dossier with the rest of your materials. The cover said, not to be read by the subject.

You still got life.

In the 2020s a graduate student applied at an archive to read the Special Court trial records. Most of her request was refused. She was allowed to copy out only a few pages by hand. One of them was what you said that afternoon. She copied it into her notebook, took it back to her dorm and read it all night.

Later, in a footnote to her thesis, she wrote that while pleading guilty the defendant gave accounts of Anting and Shanghai Diesel that differed from the indictment. On Shanghai Diesel, he said the person who protected the detainees was not himself. This statement was not accepted at the time and was not reported. At a point where the defendant could have cleared himself, he chose to say that this good deed was not his.

At her defense her adviser told her to delete the footnote. She did not delete it.

Fiction The ending of the dream “The Witness Who Told the Truth” (D3) follows the IF draft, “In Act Six, at Qincheng, choose to write an honest confession... the ending is in the Epilogue, when someone in the 2020s reads this material.” Why did it not happen in history? The Special Court trial was a political trial broadcast to the whole country, and the defendants had very little room. Wang Hongwen chose to plead guilty to everything. Who paid the price? The one who told the truth got no reduction in sentence. How long could it last? One page in an archive, one footnote.

2144:
In history, Wang Hongwen was arrested on October 6, 1976, and first held in the basement of the Great Hall of the People. In April 1977 he was moved to Qincheng Prison, and in July he was expelled from the Party. At the Special Court trial, from November 1980 to January 1981, he pleaded guilty to everything and had no lawyer. He was sentenced to life imprisonment and deprived of political rights for life. His mother died after learning of the verdict. His wife, Cui Gendi, did not divorce him and took the children to visit him at Qincheng every October 1. In 1985 he was moved to Beijing Fuxing Hospital for treatment of liver disease. He died on August 3, 1992, aged 56.

In Shanghai, Huang Jinhai, Xu Jingxian, Wang Xiuzhen, Chen Ada, Ye Changming, Zhu Yongjia and others were sentenced in 1982. Most were released in the 1990s and went back to their old factories, with their years of service reset to zero.

At daybreak more than 100 people came out of the building, lined up and left by the side gate. A few dozen refused to leave and held the roof. The crowd outside waited until noon. The order to storm the building never came, and half of them went home.

In the afternoon the fighting started anyway, on a smaller scale, and no fire trucks were called in. One person died, a young worker from the roof, who fell down the stairs.

Later some said that on August 4 a thousand people would have been hurt, and you brought it down to a few dozen. Others said you dragged something that could have ended in a day out into two months, and the Liansi people roamed around outside and hurt others. Both views had a point.

At a Workers' General Headquarters meeting, people said your stand was wrong and you were hand in glove with the royalists. That winter Zhang Chunqiao did not call you to Beijing. At National Day 1968, someone else led the Shanghai delegation.
